samf-senior-2019-r1-01.title: Avoid the traps
samf-senior-2019-r1-01.body:
Anything (non-zero) to the power 0 is 1, not 0; and 1 to any power is 1, not 2019. So the value is $1 + 3 + 1 = 5$.

**Answer: (A) 5**

samf-senior-2019-r1-02.title: Seconds in an hour
samf-senior-2019-r1-02.body:
One hour is $60\times 60 = 3600$ s, and $\frac{3600}{40} = 90$ s.

**Answer: (C) 90**

samf-senior-2019-r1-03.title: Evaluate
samf-senior-2019-r1-03.body:
$3^2 = 9$, $2^3 = 8$, $3\times 2 = 2\times 3 = 6$. So $3^2 > 2^3$ is true, and B, C ($9 \ne 6$), D ($8 < 6$ false) and E ($9 < 6$ false) are wrong.

**Answer: (A) $3^2 > 2^3$**

samf-senior-2019-r1-03.title: Only one can be right
samf-senior-2019-r1-03.body:
A and B contradict each other, and since $9 \ne 8$, B is false, so A ($9 > 8$) is the true statement.

**Answer: (A) $3^2 > 2^3$**

samf-senior-2019-r1-05.title: Parity of 7
samf-senior-2019-r1-05.body:
Consecutive Mondays are 7 days apart, an odd number. Since Harry eats fish on alternate days, if he eats fish on one Monday he does not on the next, and vice versa. Over the four Mondays the pattern is fish, no, fish, no (or the reverse): 2 Mondays.

**Answer: (B) 2**

samf-senior-2019-r1-05.title: Number the days
samf-senior-2019-r1-05.body:
Number the days $0, 1, 2, \dots, 27$ with day 0 a Monday; Mondays are days $0, 7, 14, 21$. Harry eats fish on all even days or on all odd days. Either way exactly two of $0, 7, 14, 21$ qualify (0, 14 are even; 7, 21 are odd).

**Answer: (B) 2**

samf-senior-2019-r1-06.title: Multiplication principle
samf-senior-2019-r1-06.body:
Each of the three digits can be any of 10 digits: $10\times 10\times 10 = 1000$ codes.

**Answer: (C) 1 000**

samf-senior-2019-r1-06.title: List them
samf-senior-2019-r1-06.body:
The codes are exactly $000, 001, \dots, 999$: the numbers from 0 to 999 written with three digits. There are $1000$ of them.

**Answer: (C) 1 000**

samf-senior-2019-r1-07.title: Edge length
samf-senior-2019-r1-07.body:
Six equal faces: each has area $216/6 = 36$ m$^2$, so the edge is 6 m and the volume $6^3 = 216$ m$^3$.

**Answer: (E) 216**

samf-senior-2019-r1-07.title: Formula
samf-senior-2019-r1-07.body:
$6x^2 = 216 \Rightarrow x^2 = 36 \Rightarrow x = 6$, $V = x^3 = 216$. (Coincidentally the same number as the area.)

**Answer: (E) 216**

samf-senior-2019-r1-08.title: Total distance
samf-senior-2019-r1-08.body:
In 2 hours at 280 km/h he covers $560$ km. One lap is $560/70 = 8$ km.

**Answer: (B) 8**

samf-senior-2019-r1-08.title: Laps per hour
samf-senior-2019-r1-08.body:
He does 35 laps per hour, covering 280 km per hour, so one lap is $280/35 = 8$ km.

**Answer: (B) 8**

samf-senior-2019-r1-09.title: Find the side length
samf-senior-2019-r1-09.body:
Horizontally the four squares sit side by side (each starts where the previous one ends), so from $A$ (bottom-left corner of the first) to $B$ (top-right corner of the last) the $x$-coordinate increases by four sides: $6 + 4\ell = 38$, $\ell = 8$.

$C$ is the bottom-left corner of the third square, which is two squares to the left of and two squares below $B$: $C = (38 - 2\cdot 8;\ 36 - 2\cdot 8) = (22; 20)$.

**Answer: (D) $(22; 20)$**

samf-senior-2019-r1-09.title: Work back from $B$
samf-senior-2019-r1-09.body:
With side 8 (from the $x$-coordinates as above), the fourth square has $B = (38; 36)$ as its top-right corner, so it covers $30 \le x \le 38$, $28 \le y \le 36$. The third square touches it corner to corner, so it covers $22 \le x \le 30$, $20 \le y \le 28$, and $C$ is its bottom-left corner: $(22; 20)$.

(One cannot simply work up from $A$ vertically: $7 + 4\cdot 8 = 39 \ne 36$, because the second and third squares overlap a little in height.)

**Answer: (D) $(22; 20)$**

samf-senior-2019-r1-10.title: Angles on a straight line
samf-senior-2019-r1-10.body:
Each triangle has one vertex on the horizontal line. At the left vertex the angles on the line are $75^\circ$, the triangle's $60^\circ$, and the rest: $180^\circ - 75^\circ - 60^\circ = 45^\circ$. At the right vertex: $180^\circ - 65^\circ - 60^\circ = 55^\circ$.

The two sides making these $45^\circ$ and $55^\circ$ angles form a triangle with the line, whose third angle is $180^\circ - 45^\circ - 55^\circ = 80^\circ$. That $80^\circ$ angle is vertically opposite an angle of the small triangle containing $x$, which also has a $60^\circ$ angle of an equilateral triangle. So $x = 180^\circ - 60^\circ - 80^\circ = 40^\circ$.

**Answer: (D) $40^\circ$**

samf-senior-2019-r1-10.title: Exterior angle
samf-senior-2019-r1-10.body:
With the $45^\circ$ and $55^\circ$ angles found as above, the exterior-angle theorem applied to the small triangle with angles $x$ and $60^\circ$ gives $x + 60^\circ = 45^\circ + 55^\circ$, so $x = 40^\circ$.

**Answer: (D) $40^\circ$**

samf-senior-2019-r1-11.title: Two linear equations
samf-senior-2019-r1-11.body:
$(x + y)^5 = 2^5$ gives $x + y = 2$ (the only real fifth root). $\sqrt[4]{x - y} = 2$ gives $x - y = 16$. Subtracting, $2y = -14$, so $y = -7$ (and $x = 9$).

**Answer: (B) $-7$**

samf-senior-2019-r1-12.title: Remove common multiples
samf-senior-2019-r1-12.body:
Multiples of 28 below 300: $28, 56, \dots, 280$, that is 10 numbers. A number divisible by both 28 and 12 is divisible by $\text{lcm}(28, 12) = 84$: $84, 168, 252$ (3 numbers). So $10 - 3 = 7$.

**Answer: (C) 7**

samf-senior-2019-r1-12.title: Look at the multiplier
samf-senior-2019-r1-12.body:
$28k$ is divisible by 12 iff $7k$ is divisible by 3, iff $3 \mid k$. For $k = 1, \dots, 10$, the values $k = 3, 6, 9$ are excluded, leaving 7.

**Answer: (C) 7**

samf-senior-2019-r1-13.title: Use the right pairs
samf-senior-2019-r1-13.body:
Bags 2+3 contain 43 and bags 4+5 contain 30, so bags 2 to 5 contain 73. Bag 1 contains $100 - 73 = 27$.

**Answer: (D) 27**

samf-senior-2019-r1-14.title: Most terms end in 0
samf-senior-2019-r1-14.body:
For $n \ge 5$, $n!$ contains the factors 2 and 5, so it ends in 0. The units digit is that of $1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33$, which is 3.

**Answer: (C) 3**

samf-senior-2019-r1-14.title: Running total
samf-senior-2019-r1-14.body:
Track only units digits: $1, 1+2 = 3, 3+6 = 9, 9+4 = 13 \to 3$, and every later term adds a multiple of 10. The units digit stays 3.

**Answer: (C) 3**

samf-senior-2019-r1-15.title: Substitute the fourth root
samf-senior-2019-r1-15.body:
Let $x = \sqrt[4]{N} \ge 0$, so $\sqrt N = x^2$ and $x^2 - x = 12$, i.e. $(x - 4)(x + 3) = 0$. Since $x \ge 0$, $x = 4$ and $N = 4^4 = 256$.

**Answer: (E) 256**

samf-senior-2019-r1-15.title: Test the options
samf-senior-2019-r1-15.body:
$\sqrt{256} - \sqrt[4]{256} = 16 - 4 = 12$ ✓. For 16: $4 - 2 = 2$; the others do not even have integer roots, and e.g. $\sqrt{128} - \sqrt[4]{128} \approx 11.3 - 3.4 < 12$.

**Answer: (E) 256**

samf-senior-2019-r1-16.title: Cut and rearrange
samf-senior-2019-r1-16.body:
The lower shaded region can be cut into two pieces that fit exactly into a $2\times 2$ square (the quarter-circle bulge fills the matching quarter-circle hollow), so its area is 4.

The upper shaded region is a $4\times 4$ square minus a quarter circle of radius 4: $16 - \frac14\pi\cdot 4^2 = 16 - 4\pi$.

Total: $4 + 16 - 4\pi = 20 - 4\pi$.

**Answer: (E) $20 - 4\pi$**

samf-senior-2019-r1-16.title: Estimate
samf-senior-2019-r1-16.body:
$20 - 4\pi \approx 7.4$. Counting squares in the picture, the upper shaded part covers about 3.4 squares and the lower part about 4, so about 7.4 in total. The other options are about 3.1, 6.6, 22 and 5.6.

**Answer: (E) $20 - 4\pi$**

samf-senior-2019-r1-17.title: Thales' theorem
samf-senior-2019-r1-17.body:
$E$ is equidistant from $T$, $R$, $H$, so these lie on a circle with centre $E$, and $HR = 17$ is a diameter. Hence $\angle HTR = 90^\circ$ and $TR = \sqrt{17^2 - 15^2} = \sqrt{64} = 8$.

**Answer: (D) 8**

samf-senior-2019-r1-17.title: Isosceles triangles
samf-senior-2019-r1-17.body:
Triangles $ETH$ and $ETR$ are isosceles. Their base angles $\alpha$ (at $H$ and $T$) and $\beta$ (at $R$ and $T$) satisfy $2\alpha + 2\beta = 180^\circ$, so $\angle HTR = \alpha + \beta = 90^\circ$. Then Pythagoras gives $TR = 8$ (an 8-15-17 triangle).

**Answer: (D) 8**

samf-senior-2019-r1-18.title: Give one each first
Stars and bars
samf-senior-2019-r1-18.body:
Place the 7 bananas in a row; choose 3 of the 6 gaps between them to split the row into 4 non-empty groups: $\binom63 = 20$.

**Answer: (D) 20**

samf-senior-2019-r1-20.title: Congruent and similar triangles
samf-senior-2019-r1-20.body:
Name the tilted square's vertices: $B$ at the bottom (on the dashed baseline), $A$ on the left and $C$ on the right. The small squares have sides $\sqrt{12} = 2\sqrt3$, $\sqrt3$ and $\sqrt{27} = 3\sqrt3$.

- $C$ is the top-left corner of the stack $27, 3, 12$ standing on the baseline, so its height is $CH = 3\sqrt3 + \sqrt3 + 2\sqrt3 = 6\sqrt3$ ($H$ = foot of the perpendicular on the baseline).
- Let $G$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to the baseline. Triangles $AGB$ and $BHC$ are congruent: both are right-angled, $AB = BC$, and $\angle ABG = 90^\circ - \angle CBH = \angle BCH$. So $GB = CH = 6\sqrt3$.
- $A$ is directly above the left side of the left 12-square, whose bottom corners are $G$ and $F$, so $GF = 2\sqrt3$ and $FB = 4\sqrt3$. Side $AB$ passes through the square's top-right corner $E$; let $D$ be its top-left corner. Triangles $ADE$ and $EFB$ are similar, so $\frac{AD}{DE} = \frac{EF}{FB} = \frac{2\sqrt3}{4\sqrt3} = \frac12$, giving $AD = \sqrt3$ and $AG = 3\sqrt3$.

Area of the tilted square $= AB^2 = GB^2 + AG^2 = 108 + 27 = 135$.

**Answer: (B) 135**

samf-senior-2019-r1-20.title: Trigonometry
samf-senior-2019-r1-20.body:
All right triangles in the figure are similar; let $\alpha$ be their smallest angle. The lower-right side of the tilted square is $(\sqrt{27} + \sqrt3 + \sqrt{12})\sec\alpha = 6\sqrt3\sec\alpha$. The lower-left side is made of the hypotenuses over the 12-square: $\sqrt{12}\sec\alpha + \sqrt{12}\csc\alpha$. Equal sides give $6\sec\alpha = 2\sec\alpha + 2\csc\alpha$, i.e. $2\sec\alpha = \csc\alpha$, so $\tan\alpha = \frac12$ and $\sec^2\alpha = \frac54$. The area is $(6\sqrt3)^2\sec^2\alpha = 108\cdot\frac54 = 135$.

**Answer: (B) 135**
